q: What is the strongest predictor of phantom limb pain after amputation?
o: Pain in the limb before amputation
why: Pre-amputation pain is the strongest predictor; others include proximal or bilateral amputation and poorly controlled acute pain.

q: Which intervention may reduce the incidence of phantom limb pain?
o: Peri-operative regional analgesia (epidural or perineural catheter)
why: Pre-emptive or peri-operative regional anaesthesia may reduce incidence. Ketamine may help central sensitisation.

q: What is the difference between phantom limb sensation and phantom limb pain?
o: Sensation is a non-painful awareness of the limb and is common; pain is painful and pathological
Sensation only occurs after upper limb amputation
why: Phantom sensation is very common and not pathological; phantom pain involves peripheral, spinal and cortical mechanisms.

q: Which non-pharmacological treatment is used for phantom limb pain?
why: Mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, TENS, physiotherapy and psychological support are used.

q: How is chronic post-surgical pain defined?
o: Pain at the surgical site lasting over 3 months, not explained by another cause
Any pain needing opioids at discharge
why: CPSP is pain over 3 months after surgery at the site, not explained by another cause. Severe acute pain is the strongest predictor.

q: A diabetic patient for amputation has a resting heart rate of 110 and a postural BP drop. What does this suggest?
why: Autonomic neuropathy causes resting tachycardia and postural hypotension, raising intra-operative instability and silent ischaemia risk.

q: Which type of CRPS involves a confirmed nerve injury?
why: Type 2 (previously causalgia) has a confirmed nerve injury; type 1 (most common) does not.

q: What is the main reason to use perineural catheters for amputation analgesia?
o: To give continuous analgesia for several days and possibly reduce phantom pain
To allow early discharge on day 1
They are mandatory for spinal anaesthesia
why: A surgeon-placed or ultrasound-guided sciatic catheter gives several days of analgesia; review by the pain team.

q: Which nerve blocks are usually used for below-knee amputation?
why: Sciatic plus femoral or saphenous blocks cover below-knee amputation.

q: A spinal cord stimulator patient needs surgery. What is the key concern with diathermy?
o: Tissue heating and device damage: discuss with the manufacturer or pain team beforehand
why: Diathermy is generally contraindicated near these devices; plan with the pain team and manufacturer.
